Mathematical truths are rational propositions rooted in comparisons rather than empirical observation. They are structured around numerical and spatial relationships—arithmetic from number comparisons and geometry from spatial magnitudes. Attention strokes form the basis of number, where groups of these strokes are retained and compared. This process underpins both cognitive and computational models: in GSI, such comparisons inform Bayesian inference and conformal prediction; in GSE, they enable dynamic state transitions based on grouped attention. The psychological facilitation of discrimination through mobility allows for flexible grouping, but also introduces variability depending on how entities are perceived. Thus, the foundational structure of mathematical cognition is both internal (memory-based) and relational (comparative), forming the kernel for abstract reasoning in both domains.
